title: Christmas: twelve days
hookLine: Christmas is a season, not a day, running to 6 January

lines: A PARTRIDGE IN A PEAR TREE.
cards: December twenty-sixth. Wrapping paper in bags by the door. Radio stations quietly switching back to regular music.
By New Year's, trees are lying on the curb, a little brown, a few strands of tinsel still caught in the branches. Christmas: done. Here's the surprise.
For many churches, on December twenty-sixth, Christmas has barely started. The old song about a partridge in a pear tree, with gifts piling up day after day, is counting something real.
In the church's calendar, Christmas isn't a day. It's a season, twelve days long, running up to the sixth of January. Today's word is the season, and the thing it celebrates.

teach.h: CHRIST'S MASS: THE FEAST OF CHRIST.
teach.b: Christmas. Old English, Christ's Mass: the feast of Christ. It celebrates what Christians call the incarnation, God becoming a human being.
John's Gospel says it this way: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
And Matthew gives the name the prophet promised: "Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." That's the heart of it. Not God far off, watching.
God with us, as a baby who needs feeding.
The twelve days run from Christmas Day to the eve of the sixth of January, which is Epiphany, the day the wise men arrive. And they aren't only cozy.
In Western churches, the day after Christmas remembers Stephen, whom tradition calls the first Christian martyr. A few days later, the children Herod killed in Bethlehem.
The season holds joy and grief in the same hands, like many families at the holidays. Was Jesus really born on December twenty-fifth?
The Gospels never say; they give no date at all. By the fourth century, Christians in Rome kept the feast on that day, and scholars still debate why.

Many Orthodox Christians, who follow the older Julian calendar, celebrate Christmas on what the rest of the world calls January seventh. Same feast, different calendar. Underneath, the twelve days make one point.
If God with us is true, Christians say, it's too big for one day. You don't unwrap it in an afternoon. You keep celebrating.

how: Many Christians go to church on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day and keep celebrating through the twelve days to Epiphany; many Orthodox Christians celebrate on January 7, following the Julian calendar.

practice: Think of one good thing from the last few weeks that you moved past too quickly: a kind word, a meal, a win, a laugh with someone.
Go back to it now and let yourself feel it again, slowly, the way you'd look at a gift a second time. If you pray, give thanks for it, and for God with us; if you don't, just stay with the gladness.
